text:
The first sign was not the water but the smell of a wet penny.

It appeared in the Department of Comparative Literature on a Monday in October, faintly metallic, as if it came from the radiator. The radiator was cold. By noon, three people had noticed. By two, Professor Vale had placed a blue-bird saucer beneath the window, where a bead of water had formed on the sill. The saucer, decorated with the words *A Little Something*, had come from the kitchenette. No one knew who had brought it in. It had simply always been there.

The building was called the Barlow Humanities Center, though its occupants called it Barlow. An eight-story block of buff stone and tinted glass, it stood on a slope above the river. At its opening in the late eighties, deans had posed before it in excellent coats, smiling with the confidence of people who had not yet encountered its plumbing.

The first official notice described a “localized moisture condition” near the west façade. A contractor would assess it, and faculty should continue normal operations. The message ended, *We appreciate your patience*, a phrase that would soon seem less like gratitude than a description of their character.

On Wednesday, a man in a hard hat tapped the wall beside Vale’s office with a clipboard. The exterior wall assembly, he explained, was not performing as designed.

“What does that mean?” Vale asked.

“A waterproofing layer was omitted during construction.”

“Omitted,” she repeated.

“Apparently.”

Later reports preferred “a deficiency in the original building envelope,” a phrase that left agency unresolved. Rain entered the wall, traveled sideways behind the stone, then descended and emerged far from where it began.

At an open meeting, the facilities director showed a diagram. A dashed line marked the missing membrane.

“So the wall was never waterproof?” someone asked.

“It was intended to be.”

“What’s kept the water out for thirty years?”

“The materials have, in some measure, performed.”

The room fell quiet. The director studied the slide as if it might offer a better answer.

Repairs began in November. Scaffolding rose along the west side, and a blue tarp covered the courtyard-facing wall. Workers drilled into the stone and fed hoses through openings. A saw might whine for five seconds, stop, then resume just as someone reached the sentence they were trying to understand.

At eight-thirty, Vale taught a seminar on narrative and exile. She had prepared a discussion of a novel about a family returning to a town that no longer recognized them. A drill started outside. The students raised their voices; Vale raised hers. For several minutes, they all sounded as if they were bidding at an auction.

In December, a notice announced that some offices would require “brief access coordination.” Faculty were asked to clear their walls and move belongings away from exterior surfaces. Crews would remove drywall, inspect the cavities, and apply temporary sealant. Temporary, they explained, might mean months.

Vale and her office neighbor, Dr. Nanduri, boxed their books. Between them they had thousands, many marked with notes or acquired at conferences and on students’ recommendations. The university supplied eighteen boxes.

“Do you have another?” Vale asked a worker.

“I don’t.”

“Could I get one somewhere else?”

“You can ask your administrator.”

Their administrator was home sick. Vale filled boxes, then grocery bags. One split under the weight. A passing student caught it before the books hit the floor. For a moment, they held its sagging handles together while the worker waited to move the desk.

The drywall came away in a neat rectangle. Inside lay insulation and a dark cavity that smelled of earth. A black residue lined a strip of wood near the floor, edged with faint green.

“Is that mold?” Vale asked.

“It’s not my area,” said the worker holding a camera.

A report later called it “microbial growth.” The university’s consultant took samples. The first set was inconclusive, the second delayed, and the third consistent with elevated moisture. The department was told not to disturb the cavity, not to store food nearby, and to keep the door closed when possible.

Vale’s door had never closed properly. A service request from years before had been marked complete. Now she wedged a chair against it and taught in a windowless seminar room with ventilation like a distant dishwasher. Religious Studies used it Tuesdays, Linguistics Wednesdays, and a public-speaking program whenever it had nowhere else to go. Vale could book it Thursdays, except when a visitor needed it.

The students adjusted. They carried the air of people who had learned a university might ask them to read difficult things in a room not meant for reading. One developed a cough that lasted weeks. Another said her eyes irritated whenever she worked in Vale’s office. A student with allergies called the air “a basement quality.” He had grown up in a house with a basement and did not mean it as praise.

In January, the consultant arrived in a navy jacket, carrying an instrument with a small screen. She asked Vale about symptoms.

“Some congestion. A headache once or twice.”

“Any known sensitivities?”

“Everyone has something they’re sensitive to.”

The consultant took readings. The work area, she said, was within the recommended range, though she would not advise spending extended periods near the open cavity.

“How long will it be open?”

“That depends on the contractor.”

The repair schedule was described in emails as “fluid.” Dates changed. Crews arrived, then didn’t. A wall was opened, inspected, sprayed, and covered, only to be opened again after rain. One Friday, workers removed plastic sheeting from the corridor. By Monday, it was back, held to the ceiling with blue tape.

At a February faculty meeting, the dean thanked everyone for their flexibility. The university took air quality seriously, she said, and relocation options were being explored.

“Where would we go?” Dr. Nanduri asked.

“That is being explored,” the administrator said.

“We have offices full of books. Classes. Equipment.”

“Yes,” the dean said. “Those are all factors.”

The meeting ended without a decision. Nanduri returned to his office, where his books were boxed. Vale went to the kitchenette and washed the blue-bird saucer. Beneath the window, a new drop had appeared.

In March, a storm moved through overnight. By morning, water had reached the art-history lounge, an office on the sixth floor, and a copy room below Vale. In the lounge, a ceiling tile sagged into a shallow bowl. A dehumidifier hummed beside it. People began calling the lounge the sea room.

One afternoon, the dehumidifier’s hose slipped from its drain pan, sending water across the floor. The university added fans and more plastic sheeting. The air felt dry in some places, damp in others. Vale carried cough drops and began inspecting walls before entering rooms: a bubble in the paint, a shadow, a stain she couldn’t remember seeing before. She wondered whether it was new or whether she had only learned how to look.

In April, an email announced “substantial progress.” The façade was nearly complete. Interior work would continue in stages: closing the cavities, repairing the finishes, confirming the repairs had worked. Confirmation seemed to mean waiting for rain.

The department developed its own vocabulary. No one said *mold* in front of the dean; the word seemed to provoke a correction. People said *the wall issue*, *the air concern*, *the repair situation*. They booked the conference room in pencil and asked student workers which entrances were blocked. The student workers had learned that no one knew.

Spring term ended. Faculty carried some books home and left others stacked against the walls. Vale packed a few into suitcases and took them to her apartment. They remained on the dining-room floor all summer while she worked at her kitchen table, reading manuscripts between calls from contractors and messages from colleagues.

In August, the university sent a final update. The exterior repairs were complete. Interior work would continue into fall. The affected offices had been inspected; air-quality measurements were within acceptable limits. The phrase was highlighted in blue. Nobody explained the limits or who had accepted them, but the department took the news as a cease-fire.

When Vale returned, her office had been repainted. The books were back on the shelves, though not in their old order. Someone had wiped down the desk. The wall looked smooth and clean. The smell of wet pennies was gone, or perhaps hidden beneath the new paint. Vale set down her bag and looked through the window at the green courtyard. A small rectangle of blue tarp remained at the far end of the scaffolding.

The department held its first meeting of the year in the conference room. The chair gave an update on construction, then moved on to hiring and the curriculum. Nanduri mentioned that a dehumidifier still ran in one office. The chair said she would follow up. Vale wrote it down, though the note was not for memory.

The department had not decided the building was safe. It had decided the building was the building, and life could be conducted in it while various people determined its condition. Safe, usable, finished, temporary: each word described a stage of negotiation more than a fact.

In October, rain came again, light at first, then steady through the afternoon. Vale heard it against the glass while reading a student’s essay. The blue-bird saucer sat empty beneath the window. At five, she put the essay in her bag and switched off her lamp. Water gathered on the glass and slid down in wavering threads.

The elevator was full, so she took the stairs, passing taped doors and rooms whose walls had been opened and repaired. On the landing between the third and second floors, she paused to let a group of students pass. They were talking about a novel, or a film, or someone one of them had met. Their voices rose through the stairwell and disappeared below.

Vale continued down, one hand on the rail. There would be another update: dates, delays, assurances, and, if the weather cooperated, a stretch of time when nothing seemed to be happening. She could not say she trusted the building. Trust was too large a word for a place constructed without the thing meant to keep it dry.

But there were books on the shelves again. Students would arrive in the morning. There were courses to teach, arguments to make, letters to write. Beyond the walls, however imperfectly assembled, was the future, which the department had always been asked to inhabit before it was ready.
